results.answer: A Carbon-film resistor limits electric current and creates controlled voltage drops.
The Carbon-film resistor symbol looks like a resistor zigzag or rectangle between two wires.
A Carbon-film resistor works like this: electrical energy is changed into a small amount of heat as current is limited.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that limits electric current and creates controlled voltage drops.
A Metal-film resistor limits current with stable and accurate resistance.
The Metal-film resistor symbol looks like the standard resistor zigzag or rectangle symbol.
Inside its job, a thin metal film resists charge flow and produces a predictable voltage drop.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that limits current with stable and accurate resistance.
This is a Wirewound resistor. It handles more power while limiting current.
The Wirewound resistor symbol looks like the standard resistor symbol, sometimes marked as wirewound.
Inside its job, resistance wire turns electrical energy into heat.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that handles more power while limiting current.
Potentiometer lets a user adjust resistance or divide a voltage.
The Potentiometer symbol looks like a resistor symbol touched by a movable arrow called the wiper.
A Potentiometer works like this: turning its shaft moves the wiper along a resistive track.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that lets a user adjust resistance or divide a voltage.
NTC thermistor senses temperature because its resistance changes.
The NTC thermistor symbol looks like a resistor symbol crossed by a temperature mark.
A NTC thermistor works like this: its resistance decreases when its temperature rises.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that senses temperature because its resistance changes.
Photoresistor senses light by changing resistance.
The Photoresistor symbol looks like a resistor inside a circle with arrows pointing toward it.
Inside its job, more light usually lowers its resistance.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that senses light by changing resistance.
This is a Ceramic capacitor. It stores a small charge and filters fast electrical noise.
The Ceramic capacitor symbol looks like two equal parallel plates with a gap.
A Ceramic capacitor works like this: it charges and discharges quickly and may be connected either way around.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that stores a small charge and filters fast electrical noise.
Electrolytic capacitor stores charge and smooths slower power-supply changes.
The Electrolytic capacitor symbol looks like two capacitor plates with a plus sign marking the positive side.
Inside its job, it stores more charge than many similarly sized capacitors.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that stores charge and smooths slower power-supply changes.
Tantalum capacitor provides stable capacitance in a small package.
The Tantalum capacitor symbol looks like a polarized capacitor symbol with its positive terminal marked.
Inside its job, a tantalum dielectric stores charge in a compact part.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that provides stable capacitance in a small package.
This is a Film capacitor. It stores charge with low loss and good stability.
The Film capacitor symbol looks like two equal capacitor plates with a gap.
Inside its job, plastic film separates conducting layers that hold opposite charges.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that stores charge with low loss and good stability.
This is a Supercapacitor. It stores much more charge than an ordinary capacitor.
The Supercapacitor symbol looks like a polarized capacitor symbol, often labelled with capacitance and polarity.
A Supercapacitor works like this: it charges and discharges repeatedly between a capacitor and a small battery in behavior.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that stores much more charge than an ordinary capacitor.
This is a Ferrite-core inductor. It stores energy in a magnetic field and resists sudden current change.
Look for a row of curved wire loops; that is the Ferrite-core inductor symbol.
Inside its job, current through its coil builds a magnetic field in the ferrite core.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that stores energy in a magnetic field and resists sudden current change.
A Air-core inductor stores magnetic energy without a magnetic core.
The Air-core inductor symbol looks like a row of curved wire loops without core lines.
A Air-core inductor works like this: its coil creates a magnetic field mostly through air.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that stores magnetic energy without a magnetic core.
Transformer moves alternating-current energy between circuits and changes voltage.
Look for two coils facing each other, often with core lines between them; that is the Transformer symbol.
Inside its job, changing current in one coil creates a changing magnetic field that induces voltage in the other.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that moves alternating-current energy between circuits and changes voltage.
This is a Cartridge fuse. It opens a circuit when current stays dangerously high.
The Cartridge fuse symbol looks like a small rectangle placed in series with a wire.
A Cartridge fuse works like this: its thin internal link melts and stops current.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that opens a circuit when current stays dangerously high.
Resettable fuse reduces current when it becomes too hot from an overload.
The Resettable fuse symbol looks like a resistor-like protection symbol commonly labelled PTC.
A Resettable fuse works like this: its resistance rises sharply during an overload and falls after cooling.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that reduces current when it becomes too hot from an overload.
Rectifier diode allows current mainly in one direction.
The Rectifier diode symbol looks like a diode triangle-like wedge shape pointing toward a straight bar.
Inside its job, it conducts when forward biased and blocks most reverse current.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that allows current mainly in one direction.
A Zener diode holds an approximate voltage when used in reverse breakdown.
The Zener diode symbol looks like a diode symbol with a bent cathode bar.
A Zener diode works like this: it blocks reverse current until its Zener voltage is reached, then conducts.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that holds an approximate voltage when used in reverse breakdown.
A Schottky diode passes current in one direction with a relatively small voltage drop.
The Schottky diode symbol looks like a diode symbol with a hooked cathode marking.
Inside its job, a metal-semiconductor junction switches quickly.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that passes current in one direction with a relatively small voltage drop.
This is a Light-emitting diode. It turns electrical energy into light.
The Light-emitting diode symbol looks like a diode symbol with two arrows pointing outward.
A Light-emitting diode works like this: forward current makes its semiconductor junction emit light.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that turns electrical energy into light.
This is a Photodiode. It turns light into a small electrical current.
The Photodiode symbol looks like a diode symbol with arrows pointing inward.
Inside its job, incoming light creates charge carriers in its junction.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that turns light into a small electrical current.
A NPN transistor uses a small base current to control a larger collector current.
The NPN transistor symbol looks like a three-terminal transistor whose emitter arrow points outward.
A NPN transistor works like this: base current allows current to flow between collector and emitter.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that uses a small base current to control a larger collector current.
A PNP transistor switches or amplifies using opposite polarities to an NPN transistor.
The PNP transistor symbol looks like a three-terminal transistor whose emitter arrow points outward.
Inside its job, pulling its base below its emitter allows collector current.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that switches or amplifies using opposite polarities to an NPN transistor.
A N-channel MOSFET uses gate voltage to control current between drain and source.
The N-channel MOSFET symbol looks like a three-terminal field-effect transistor with an insulated gate.
Inside its job, sufficient positive gate-to-source voltage forms a conducting channel.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that uses gate voltage to control current between drain and source.
P-channel MOSFET switches a positive supply using gate voltage.
The P-channel MOSFET symbol looks like a MOSFET symbol with the P-channel arrow direction.
Inside its job, pulling the gate below the source turns its channel on.
Mystery round! Pick the hero where pulling the gate below the source turns its channel on.
A IGBT switches high voltage or current using an insulated control gate.
The IGBT symbol looks like a power transistor symbol combining MOS gate and bipolar output features.
Inside its job, gate voltage controls a bipolar current path.
Mystery round! Pick the hero where gate voltage controls a bipolar current path.
A SPST switch manually connects or disconnects one circuit path.
The SPST switch symbol looks like two contacts with one movable line between them.
Inside its job, closing joins the contacts; opening separates them.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that manually connects or disconnects one circuit path.
This is a Momentary push button. It changes a circuit only while it is being pressed.
The Momentary push button symbol looks like switch contacts with a push actuator mark.
A Momentary push button works like this: a spring returns its contacts when released.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that changes a circuit only while it is being pressed.
Electromagnetic relay uses a coil signal to move separate switch contacts.
The Electromagnetic relay symbol looks like a coil drawn beside mechanically linked contacts.
Inside its job, coil current creates a magnetic field that pulls the contact arm.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that uses a coil signal to move separate switch contacts.
A Optocoupler passes a signal using light while keeping circuits electrically separated.
The Optocoupler symbol looks like an LED facing a light sensor inside one outline.
A Optocoupler works like this: the input LED shines on an internal phototransistor or photodiode.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that passes a signal using light while keeping circuits electrically separated.
A Operational amplifier amplifies the difference between two input voltages.
Look for a triangle with plus and minus inputs and one output; that is the Operational amplifier symbol.
A Operational amplifier works like this: feedback makes it perform useful analogue operations.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that amplifies the difference between two input voltages.
This is a Voltage comparator. It reports which of two input voltages is higher.
Look for a triangle with plus and minus inputs and a digital-like output; that is the Voltage comparator symbol.
Inside its job, its output changes state when the input order reverses.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that reports which of two input voltages is higher.
This is a 555 timer. It creates delays, pulses, or repeating oscillations.
The 555 timer symbol looks like an eight-pin block commonly labelled 555.
A 555 timer works like this: internal comparators watch a timing capacitor and switch the output.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that creates delays, pulses, or repeating oscillations.
This is a 7805 voltage regulator. It produces a regulated five-volt output from a higher input voltage.
The 7805 voltage regulator symbol looks like a three-pin regulator block marked input, ground, and output.
Inside its job, it continuously adjusts an internal pass device to hold the output near five volts.
Mystery round! Pick the hero where it continuously adjusts an internal pass device to hold the output near five volts.
A LM317 voltage regulator produces an adjustable regulated output voltage.
The LM317 voltage regulator symbol looks like a three-pin block marked input, output, and adjust.
A LM317 voltage regulator works like this: two external resistors set the feedback voltage.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that produces an adjustable regulated output voltage.
Buck converter efficiently changes a higher direct voltage into a lower one.
The Buck converter symbol looks like a switching power block associated with an inductor, diode or switches, and capacitor.
A Buck converter works like this: rapid switching controls energy sent through an inductor to the output.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that efficiently changes a higher direct voltage into a lower one.
Boost converter changes a lower direct voltage into a higher one.
The Boost converter symbol looks like a switching power block with an inductor and output diode or synchronous switch.
A Boost converter works like this: an inductor stores energy and then releases it at a higher voltage.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that changes a lower direct voltage into a higher one.
A L298N motor controller controls the direction and speed of two small direct-current motors.
Look for a multi-pin driver block with logic inputs and paired motor outputs; that is the L298N motor controller symbol.
A L298N motor controller works like this: internal transistor bridges reverse motor current direction and PWM can adjust a
Circuit Quest: choose the part that controls the direction and speed of two small direct-current motors.
A AND gate outputs one only when all required inputs are one.
The AND gate symbol looks like a flat-left, rounded-right logic-gate shape.
A AND gate works like this: it combines yes-or-no signals using the AND truth table.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that outputs one only when all required inputs are one.
A NOT gate outputs the opposite logic state from its input.
Look for a triangle with a small inversion circle on its output; that is the NOT gate symbol.
Inside its job, a low input produces high output and a high input produces low output.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that outputs the opposite logic state from its input.
D flip-flop stores one digital bit when triggered by a clock edge.
Look for a rectangular logic block with D, clock, Q, and often inverted-Q pins; that is the D flip-flop symbol.
Inside its job, on the active clock edge, the D input is copied to Q.
Mystery round! Pick the hero where on the active clock edge, the D input is copied to Q.
A Microcontroller runs instructions, reads inputs, and controls outputs.
Look for a rectangular integrated-circuit block with many named pins; that is the Microcontroller symbol.
A Microcontroller works like this: its processor executes code while peripherals handle timing, communication, and signals.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that runs instructions, reads inputs, and controls outputs.
A Quartz crystal provides a stable oscillation frequency for clocks.
The Quartz crystal symbol looks like a small rectangle between two capacitor-like plates.
A Quartz crystal works like this: quartz mechanically vibrates at a precise resonant frequency.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that provides a stable oscillation frequency for clocks.
This is a Hall-effect sensor. It detects a magnetic field and produces an electrical signal.
The Hall-effect sensor symbol looks like a sensor block marked with magnetic-field direction or Hall notation.
Inside its job, a magnetic field pushes charge sideways inside the sensing material.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that detects a magnetic field and produces an electrical signal.
This is a Temperature sensor. It turns temperature into a voltage, resistance, or digital reading.
The Temperature sensor symbol looks like a sensor block associated with a thermometer mark.
Inside its job, a temperature-sensitive element changes an electrical property.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that turns temperature into a voltage, resistance, or digital reading.
This is a Ultrasonic distance sensor. It measures distance using sound above human hearing.
The Ultrasonic distance sensor symbol looks like a sensor block with transmit and receive transducers.
Inside its job, it times how long an ultrasonic echo takes to return.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that measures distance using sound above human hearing.
Rotary encoder reports turning direction and movement as pulses.
The Rotary encoder symbol looks like a shaft or knob connected to two phase-shifted signal contacts.
A Rotary encoder works like this: two outputs pulse in a sequence that reveals direction.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that reports turning direction and movement as pulses.
A Battery provides direct voltage from stored chemical energy.
The Battery symbol looks like alternating long and short parallel lines marked positive and negative.
A Battery works like this: chemical reactions push charge through an external circuit.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that provides direct voltage from stored chemical energy.
A Board connector joins power or signals between wires and circuit boards.
The Board connector symbol looks like a group of numbered contacts inside a connector outline.
A Board connector works like this: matching metal contacts make removable electrical paths.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that joins power or signals between wires and circuit boards.
A Solderless breadboard lets parts and jumper wires form temporary circuits without solder.
The Solderless breadboard symbol looks like it normally has no single circuit symbol because it is a construction tool.
A Solderless breadboard works like this: hidden metal clips connect groups of holes in rows and power rails.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that lets parts and jumper wires form temporary circuits without solder.
This is a DC motor. It turns direct-current electrical energy into rotation.
The DC motor symbol looks like a circle marked M with two electrical terminals.
Inside its job, current in coils interacts with magnetic fields to create torque.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that turns direct-current electrical energy into rotation.
A Servo motor moves its shaft toward a commanded angle.
The Servo motor symbol looks like a motor or actuator block with power, ground, and control connections.
A Servo motor works like this: internal feedback compares shaft position with command pulses.
Circuit Quest: choose the part that moves its shaft toward a commanded angle.
